displayQuote: After Nirvana, we still have to chop wood and carry water

meta.title: Who really said "After Nirvana, we still have to chop wood and carry water"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not the Buddha — the imagery is Chinese Ch'an, not Indian Buddhism. It descends from Layman Pang (d. 808): 'supernatural powers and marvellous activity — fetching water and carrying firewood.' The before/after wording is modern and anonymous.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'After Nirvana, we still have to chop wood and carry water'?
meta.ogDescription: Wrong tradition, wrong millennium. The wood and water come from a Chinese Ch'an layman who died in 808 CE — about thirteen centuries after the Buddha, in a different language.

answer.label: Nobody in the Buddhist canon — a modern phrasing of a Ch'an image
answer.authorDates: Modern wording, anonymous · the underlying image is Chinese Ch'an, c. 785–808 CE
answer.sourceLine: There is no Pali source, and there could not easily be one: chopping wood and carrying water as a figure for enlightened ordinariness is Chinese Ch’an vocabulary, not Indian Buddhist vocabulary. The genuine ancestor is a couplet by the layman Pang Yun (龐蘊, d. 808) — 神通並妙用　運水及搬柴, ‘supernatural powers and marvellous activity: fetching water and carrying firewood.’ The familiar before-and-after English formula has no canonical source in any language and appears to be a twentieth-century Western formulation.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Chinese Ch’an — not the Pali canon

source.excerpt: 神通並妙用　運水及搬柴
trail: We looked for an original-language text, which is the fastest test there is. For the Buddha attribution there is none — no Pali passage pairs nibbāna with woodcutting, and the suttas do not treat nibbāna as a completed event you live on the far side of.

For the Ch’an line there is one. Pang Yun’s couplet survives in Chinese — 神通並妙用　運水及搬柴 — attached to his meeting with Shitou Xiqian around 785 CE. He was a married householder, not a monk, which is exactly why the image is about domestic chores on Layman Pang ↗.

The English everyone quotes from Pang is modern and in copyright — the standard version is Sasaki, Iriya and Fraser’s The Recorded Sayings of Layman P’ang (1971), with later renderings by James Green and Andrew Ferguson. We found no public-domain English of the couplet, so we print the Chinese the Chinese text ↗.

The before/after scaffolding — ‘before enlightenment… after enlightenment…’ — is a separate borrowing. That three-stage rhetorical shape belongs to Qingyuan Weixin’s mountains-and-waters passage, popularised in English by D. T. Suzuki. Somebody, at some point, welded Pang’s chores onto Qingyuan’s structure and signed the Buddha’s name to it. We have not been able to date that weld, and we will not invent a date for it.
source.excerptNote: Pang’s couplet in Chinese. The joke, and it is a joke, is in the first line: he announces supernatural powers and marvellous activity, then tells you what they consist of — hauling the water and lugging the firewood. Note that he is not talking about life after anything. He is talking about right now.

sourceLink.text: The Recorded Sayings of Layman Pang — Chinese and English

source.rightsNote: Split, and it matters which half you take. Pang’s Chinese couplet is ancient and free to reproduce; the English versions you will find are not. The standard translation is Ruth Fuller Sasaki, Yoshitaka Iriya and Dana R. Fraser’s (Weatherhill, 1971), and the other current renderings — James Green’s and Andrew Ferguson’s — are equally in copyright. We located no public-domain English of the verse, which is why this page quotes the Chinese and paraphrases rather than lifting a translator’s wording. The modern before/after sentence is of unknown authorship, which is not the same as being free. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Gautama Buddha
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on the Buddha
author.metaLine: fl. c. 5th century BCE · founder of Buddhism · northern India
author.bio: Siddhārtha Gautama taught in northern India in about the fifth century BCE, in an Indic vernacular, and what survives of him survives in Pali. Chinese Ch’an — the tradition that produced Layman Pang, the kōan literature and this image of wood and water — developed more than a thousand years later, in another country and another language, out of Buddhism’s meeting with Chinese thought. Crediting a Ch’an epigram to the Buddha is a bit like crediting a medieval Provençal love song to Cicero: same civilisation, wildly different address.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: The questioner who brought this to us already suspected it was Zen rather than the Buddha. That instinct is right, and the trail is unusually clean once you look for an original-language text.

items.why: No sutta, no verse, no commentary. The vocabulary is wrong twice over: firewood-and-water as a figure for enlightened ordinariness is Chinese, and nibbāna in the Pali texts is not framed as a stage you finish and then live after.

Pang’s couplet says his supernatural powers are fetching water and carrying firewood. That is a claim about the present, made by a householder about his own chores. The modern saying converts it into consolation about the day after your big moment, which is a friendlier and much smaller idea the couplet ↗.

items.who: Borrowed from a different Ch'an passage
items.why: ‘Before enlightenment… after enlightenment…’ is the structure of Qingyuan Weixin’s famous report that mountains were mountains, then were not mountains, then were really mountains again. Two separate Ch’an sources have been spliced into one sentence.

We could find no documented first appearance of the English formula — not in Quote Investigator, not on Wikiquote’s list of things wrongly credited to the Buddha. A confident-sounding invented date is exactly the error this site exists to correct, so we leave it open.

misattribution.truthLine: Not the Buddha. The wood and water come from the Chinese Ch’an layman Pang Yun, who died in 808 CE; the before-and-after wording is modern, anonymous and undated who Pang was ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is the best possible answer to the fear that enlightenment would make you useless. Whatever happens in your head, the bins still go out on Tuesday — and the saying promises that this is not a disappointment but the whole point.

The reason it gets the Buddha’s name is simple market forces. It is a Buddhist-sounding thought and he is the only Buddhist most people can name, so the credit drifts upward to the biggest available signature. Pang, who was a layman with a wife and a daughter and no monastery, is a far better fit for a saying about chores.
context.detailsSummary: The Ch'an line, and what it actually claims
detailsBody: Pang Yun (龐蘊) died in 808 CE. He was a married householder who studied under Shitou Xiqian and Mazu Daoyi and never ordained.
His couplet reads 神通並妙用　運水及搬柴 — the miraculous powers, and then the water and the firewood.
The rhetorical trick is deflation: the grand phrase is set up and then cashed out in chores.
Every English version of it in circulation was made in the last sixty years and is in copyright.
Nothing in the couplet mentions nirvana, before, or after.
context.pull: Pang was not describing life after enlightenment. He was describing the chores as the thing itself.
